events.title: World's oldest known indigo-dyed cloth
events.place: Huaca Prieta, Chicama Valley, north coast of Peru
events.summary: Cotton fabrics from the Preceramic mound of Huaca Prieta kept traces of a blue pigment that high-performance liquid chromatography identified as indigotin. The oldest indigo-bearing specimen comes from a layer bracketed by radiocarbon-dated strata, and the authors put it at about 6,200 to 6,000 years old. They attribute the dye most likely to Indigofera species native to South America (Splitstoser, Dillehay, Wouters and Claro, Science Advances, 2016).
events.significance: Shows indigo dyeing was invented in the Americas roughly 1,500 years before the earliest reported Old World evidence.

sources.title: Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru (Splitstoser, Dillehay, Wouters, Claro)
sources.quote: Because of unusual circumstances of preservation, 6000-year-old cotton fabrics from the Preceramic site of Huaca Prieta on the north coast of Peru retained traces of a blue pigment that was analyzed and positively identified as an indigoid dye (indigotin), making it the earliest known use of indigo in the world, derived most likely from Indigofera spp. native to South America.

sources.title: The Super-Ancient Origins of Your Blue Jeans (Kristin Romey)
sources.quote: ranged in age from 6,200 to around 1,500 years old

events.title: Egypt's earliest indigo-dyed linen
events.place: Egypt, Old Kingdom (Fifth Dynasty); findspot not named in the sources
events.summary: Until 2016 the oldest known indigo-dyed textiles were Egyptian linens of the Fifth Dynasty, dated to about 2400 BCE (c. 4,400 years before present). The sources consulted do not name the findspot or say whether the blue came from woad or an Indigofera species. The PROTA plant database notes that both were available to ancient Egyptians.
events.significance: The earliest reported use of indigo blue in the Old World.

sources.title: Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru
sources.quote: This predates by ~1500 years the earliest reported use of indigo in the Old World, from Fifth Dynasty Egypt [ca. 4400 BP (before present)].

sources.quote: The blue dye used for textiles of Egyptian mummies may, in some cases, come from an Indigofera species but woad ( Isatis tinctoria L.) is another indigo-blue producing plant known to ancient Egyptians.

events.title: Anatolia's oldest blue-dyed textile
events.place: Beycesultan Höyük, Çivril Plain, Denizli Province, Türkiye
events.summary: A Middle Bronze Age fragment from Beycesultan, dated to about 1915-1745 BCE, is a hemp fabric made by nålbinding (single-needle looping) and dyed with indigo from woad, according to a Koç University team. The results were published in Antiquity (DOI 10.15184/aqy.2024.194). A second hemp fragment of c. 1700-1595 BCE is a plain tabby weave.
events.significance: Places woad-indigo dyeing in Anatolia in the early second millennium BCE, close to the plant's presumed south-west Asian homeland.

sources.institution: Koç University press release via EurekAlert! (AAAS)
sources.title: Earliest evidence of indigo-dyed textiles and single-needle knitting discovered in Bronze Age Anatolia
sources.quote: Even more remarkable, the hemp fabric was dyed with indigo from the woad plant, making it the oldest blue-dyed textile discovered in Bronze Age Anatolia.

events.title: Indigo and madder on Tutankhamun's linen
events.place: Tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62), Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
events.summary: A 2023 study of a linen fragment from Tutankhamun's tomb, now at the Grand Egyptian Museum's conservation centre, combined gel micro-extraction with reflectance and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy. It identified both indigo and madder. The method detects the indigotin molecule, not the plant it came from, so the fragment cannot say whether woad or an Indigofera species was used.
events.significance: Confirms indigo blue in the textiles of a New Kingdom royal burial.

sources.quote: The combination of information deriving from FORS and SERS spectra resulted in the successful identification of both indigo and madder and, in hypothesis, of their degradation products.

events.displayDate: Bronze and Iron Ages (textiles up to c. 3,500 years old)
events.title: Woad blues from the Hallstatt salt mines
events.place: Hallstatt salt mine, Upper Austria
events.summary: Around 700 prehistoric fabric fragments, mostly wool, survive in the Hallstatt salt mines. Many are striped or checked in blue and other colours. Chromatographic analysis found indigotin, and the Natural History Museum Vienna says woad was the blue dye used in Bronze Age and Hallstatt-period Europe, sometimes applied to cloth after weaving. A 2015 study reported indigotin in 33% of the Bronze Age textiles and 58% of the Iron Age textiles analysed, while cautioning that analysis identifies the dye, not the plant.
events.significance: Vat-dyeing with woad was established in central Europe by the Bronze Age, long before the medieval woad industry.

sources.institution: Naturhistorisches Museum Wien (Natural History Museum Vienna)
sources.title: Hallstatt textiles: Colors and dyeing
sources.quote: During the Bronze Age and Hallstatt Period in Europe woad would have been used.

events.title: Cuneiform recipes for blue wool
events.place: Babylonia (southern Mesopotamia); tablet now in the British Museum
events.summary: A Late Babylonian cuneiform tablet of the seventh century BCE in the British Museum (two joined fragments, BM 62788+82978; registration 1882,0918.2757) records recipes for dyeing wool. Its formulas start with pale- or dark-blue wool (uqnâtu) produced by repeated immersion in a dye bath, then over-dye it with madder to imitate the prestige colours takiltu (blue-purple) and argamannu (red-purple). The tablet does not name the blue dye plant; the chemist Zvi Koren suggests woad. One fragment was published by Erle Leichty in 1979.
events.significance: One of the oldest surviving written dye recipes, showing blue vat-dyed wool made locally in Mesopotamia as a cheaper substitute for imported luxury colours.

sources.title: Tekhelet: Setting the Ancient Record Straight (Zvi C. Koren), Tradition 54:1
sources.quote: The British Museum has a unique seventh century BCE Late Babylonian tablet with cuneiform text containing various dyeing recipes.

sources.title: tablet, museum number 1882,0918.2757 (collection online)

events.title: Xunzi: 'Blue comes from indigo'
events.place: Warring States China (Xunzi died at Lanling, state of Chu, in present-day Shandong)
events.summary: The Confucian philosopher Xunzi (c. 300-c. 230 BCE) opens his essay 'Encouraging Learning' (Quan xue) with the line 青，取之於藍而青於藍: blue is taken from the indigo plant (lan) yet is bluer than the plant. The image assumes readers knew that a deeper blue could be extracted from indigo leaves.
events.significance: One of the earliest securely datable Chinese references to indigo dye; the line became a proverb for a pupil surpassing the teacher.

sources.title: 荀子 / 勸學篇 (Xunzi, Encouraging Learning)

sources.title: Xunzi

events.title: Caesar: Britons stain themselves blue
events.place: Britain (Cantium, modern Kent, England)
events.summary: Describing Britain at the time of his second expedition (54 BCE), Julius Caesar wrote in the Gallic War (5.14): 'Omnes vero se Britanni vitro inficiunt, quod caeruleum efficit colorem' (all the Britons stain themselves with vitrum, which produces a blue colour). Vitrum has traditionally been translated as woad, but it usually means glass. Scholars still debate whether a plant dye or a copper- or iron-based pigment was meant, and analyses of the Lindow bog bodies have not settled the question.
events.significance: The most-cited classical text linking woad to Europe, though its meaning is contested.

sources.title: Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico, Book 5
sources.quote: Omnes vero se Britanni vitro inficiunt, quod caeruleum efficit colorem, atque hoc horridiores sunt in pugna aspectu

sources.title: Cassivellaunus
sources.quote: Cassivellaunus (flourished 1st century bc) was a powerful British chieftain who was defeated by Julius Caesar during his second raiding expedition into Britain (54 bc).

sources.quote: When body painting amid the Britons is considered, two chief materials are suggested: woad ( I. Tinctoria ) and copper-based pigments.

events.title: Indigo shipped from the Indus delta
events.place: Barbarikon, Indus delta, near modern Karachi, Pakistan (exact site uncertain)
events.summary: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide to Red Sea and Indian Ocean ports written in the mid-first century CE, lists indigo among the exports of Barbarikon at the mouth of the Indus (section 39). It appears alongside costus, bdellium, nard, turquoise, lapis lazuli, cotton cloth and silk yarn.
events.significance: Documents indigo as an Indian export commodity in Roman-era Indian Ocean trade.

sources.title: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (trans. W. H. Schoff, 1912), section 39
sources.quote: On the other hand there are exported costus, bdellium, lycium, nard, turquoise, lapis lazuli, Seric skins, cotton cloth, silk yarn, and indigo.

sources.institution: Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford (Yousef Jameel Centre, Eastern Art Online)

events.title: Pliny prices Indian indigo at 20 denarii a pound
events.place: Rome, Italy
events.summary: In his Natural History (completed 77 CE), Pliny the Elder calls indicum 'a production of India' that looks black as a powder but gives a mix of purple and blue in water. He warns that it was adulterated, including with chalk coloured with woad, and states: 'The price of indicum is twenty denarii per pound.' About a century earlier, Vitruvius (writing after 27 BCE) had noted that painters short of indigo dyed chalk with woad to imitate it.
events.significance: One of the earliest recorded prices for indigo, showing it reached Rome as a costly imported pigment with woad as the cheap local substitute.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 35.27 (Bostock & Riley trans., 1855; = 35.46 in Loeb numbering)

events.displayDate: Late Preclassic period (roughly the last centuries BCE)
events.title: Earliest Maya Blue, at Calakmul
events.place: Calakmul, Campeche, Mexico
events.summary: Maya Blue is a durable pigment made by binding indigo to the clay mineral palygorskite. Physicochemical analysis identified it on a painted frieze of Late Preclassic date at Calakmul, the earliest known occurrence (Vázquez de Ágredos Pascual, Doménech-Carbó and Doménech-Carbó, Journal of Cultural Heritage, 2011). The year given here is a representative midpoint of the period, not a date for the frieze.
events.significance: Shows Mesoamerican indigo had become the basis of an advanced pigment technology by the end of the first millennium BCE.

events.title: Diocletian's price edict caps indigo at 750 denarii a pound
events.place: Roman Empire (copies survive from the eastern provinces); Diocletian's capital Nicomedia shown
events.summary: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices, issued between 20 November and 10 December 301 CE to check inflation, allows at most 750 denarii for a pound of an item translated as 'Indigo (?)' in its section on drugs, paints and dyes. That is close to the 800 denarii allowed for a pound of pepper. The edict also caps a hide dyed indigo at 400 denarii. The translator marks the identification of the indigo entry as uncertain.
events.significance: A rare fixed price point showing indigo as a high-value import in late Roman markets.

events.title: China's step-by-step recipe for indigo paste
events.place: Northern China (Eastern Wei); author Jia Sixie was from Shouguang, Shandong
events.summary: Chapter 53, 'Growing indigo', of Jia Sixie's farming manual Qimin yaoshu (completed around 544 CE) gives a full method. In the seventh month the cut plants are steeped under water in a lined pit, then the liquor is moved to jars. Lime is added at 1 dou 5 sheng per 10-shi jar and the mixture is beaten, and the settled sediment is kept as indigo paste (lan dian). The text adds that ten mu of indigo are worth a qing (100 mu) of grain land, and that growers who dye cloth themselves double their profit again.
events.significance: An early and detailed account of the lime-precipitation method of making indigo, with an explicit statement that indigo was far more lucrative per unit of land than grain.

sources.title: 齊民要術 / 卷第五, 種藍第五十三 (Qimin yaoshu, vol. 5, ch. 53)

events.title: Knotweed indigo in the Shōsōin treasures
events.place: Shōsōin repository, Tōdai-ji, Nara, Japan
events.summary: Non-destructive spectroscopy of 8th-century textiles in the Shōsōin, including a sleeveless coat used in a Buddhist ceremony in 752 CE, distinguished five dyes. Among them was 'ai blue (knotweed)', indigo from the Japanese indigo plant. Most of the repository's contents were dedicated to the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji by Empress Kōmyō in 756.
events.significance: Scientific confirmation that knotweed indigo (Persicaria tinctoria), not Indigofera, was used in Nara-period Japan.

events.title: Charlemagne's estates must supply woad
events.place: Carolingian royal estates (court at Aachen, Germany)
events.summary: The Capitulare de villis, Charlemagne's ordinance on running the royal estates, orders stewards to deliver materials for the women's textile workshops. Chapter 43 lists 'linen, wool, woad, vermilion, madder', along with wool combs, teasels and soap. A local-history source dates the text to 795; the Fordham translation gives only the 9th century.
events.significance: Shows woad was a routine, managed input of estate textile production in Carolingian Europe.

events.title: Woad seeds in the Oseberg ship burial
events.place: Oseberg mound, Slagen, near Tønsberg, Norway
events.summary: The Oseberg ship burial, dated by tree rings to 834, contained a box of woad seeds among its grave goods. The Norwegian national encyclopedia takes this as evidence that woad was grown in Viking-age Norway. The grave also held woollen textiles, imported silks and pictorial tapestries.
events.significance: Evidence that woad cultivation, and blue dyeing with it, had spread to Scandinavia by the Viking Age.

events.title: Viking-age dyers at York's Coppergate
events.place: 16-22 Coppergate, York, England
events.summary: Excavations at 16-22 Coppergate recovered 1,147 textile-production artefacts together with raw fibres and dyestuffs. Dyeing is well represented in the 9th-10th centuries and fades from the site during the 11th. Plant remains from the site include woad (Isatis tinctoria): an archaeobotanical report on mid-to-late 11th-century deposits says woad pod fragments 'may indicate continued dyeing activity'.
events.significance: Shows woad dyeing as an urban craft in Anglo-Scandinavian England.

events.title: Indigo in the Cairo Geniza: Fustat to Qayrawan
events.place: Qayrawan (Kairouan), Tunisia; goods shipped from Fustat (Old Cairo), Egypt
events.summary: A Hebrew court record from Qayrawan dated 4738 AM (977-978 CE), preserved in the Cairo Geniza (Cambridge, T-S 12.468), concerns a shipment of indigo sent from Fustat that belonged to a dead merchant. Other Geniza documents include an account headed 'what was sold from the Indian indigo (al-nīl al-hindī)'. A letter of about 1057 complains that merchants from Alexandria were flooding the market with indigo.
events.significance: Shows indigo as a routine commodity in the 10th-11th-century Jewish and Islamic Mediterranean trade that linked Egypt, North Africa and India.

events.title: Gujarati indigo-resist cottons reach Egypt
events.place: Found in Egypt (Fustat and the Red Sea port of Quseir al-Qadim); made in Gujarat, India
events.summary: The Ashmolean Museum's Newberry collection holds Indian block-printed, resist- and mordant-dyed cottons found in Egypt. Radiocarbon tests in 1994-95 gave dates as early as 1010 CE (plus or minus 55 years), and every blue textile analysed showed traces of indigotin. Designs link the cloths to Gujarat, and 53 Indian textiles were excavated at the Red Sea port of Quseir al-Qadim.
events.significance: Physical evidence of Indian indigo-dyed cotton traded to the Islamic Mediterranean from the early 11th century.

events.title: West Africa's oldest indigo textiles
events.place: Tellem burial caves, Bandiagara Escarpment, Mali
events.summary: Cotton textiles from Tellem burial caves in the Bandiagara cliff are the oldest known from sub-Saharan Africa. Some date to the 11th or 12th century and already show stripes, checks and tie-dye patterns in indigo from Indigofera or Philenoptera species. The Metropolitan Museum reports that about 500 textiles from 13 cave burial contexts were carbon-14 dated, the earliest to the eleventh century.
events.significance: The earliest firm evidence of West Africa's indigo-dyed cotton tradition.

events.title: Benjamin of Tudela's Jewish dyers
events.place: Jerusalem
events.summary: The Navarrese traveller Benjamin of Tudela, whose journey his editor dates to between 1166 and 1171, recorded Jewish dyers in southern Italy and the Levant: about ten at Brindisi and one or two at Ludd, Bethlehem, Jaffa and other towns. In Jerusalem he found 'a dyeing-house, for which the Jews pay a small rent annually to the king, on condition that besides the Jews no other dyers be allowed in Jerusalem.' He does not say which dyestuffs they used.
events.significance: Records the prominence of Jewish communities in the medieval Mediterranean dyeing trade, in which indigo was a staple.

sources.title: The Itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela (trans. and ed. M. N. Adler, 1907)
sources.quote: It contains a dyeing-house, for which the Jews pay a small rent annually to the king, on condition that besides the Jews no other dyers be allowed in Jerusalem.

events.displayDate: c. 600-1200 CE (Chichén Itzá's florescence; Maya Blue used c. 300-1500 CE)
events.title: Maya Blue made in ritual at the Sacred Cenote
events.place: Sacred Cenote, Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
events.summary: Researchers from Wheaton College and the Field Museum (Antiquity, 2008) concluded that at Chichén Itzá, Maya Blue was made during rituals beside the Sacred Cenote by burning copal incense, palygorskite and probably indigo leaves together. They linked this to the thick layer of blue sediment found when the cenote was dredged in the early 20th century. Their release says Maya Blue was used across Mesoamerica from about 300 to 1500 CE.
events.significance: Shows indigo in Mesoamerica was a ritual and sacred material, not only a textile dye.

sources.institution: Wheaton College and The Field Museum, via ScienceDaily

events.title: Woad money builds Amiens Cathedral
events.place: Amiens Cathedral, Picardy, France
events.summary: Woad, called waide or guède in Picardy, is recorded in the Somme from 1105, and its trade made Amiens rich. The cathedral's own site says the woad trade 'helped finance a large part of the work' on the building begun in 1220. A sculpture on the south side shows two woad merchants beside a sack of woad.
events.significance: Shows how medieval woad profits paid for civic and religious monuments in northern Europe.

sources.quote: The waide, as it was known in Picardy (the woad, Isatis tinctoria), a blue dye plant that produced the royal blue, helped finance a large part of the work thanks to its flourishing trade.

events.title: Chinese trade official records Gujarat's indigo exports
events.place: Gujarat, India (described from Quanzhou, China); Cambay/Khambhat shown
events.summary: Zhao Rugua (Chau Ju-kua), supervisor of maritime trade at Quanzhou, finished his Zhu fan zhi (Records of Foreign Peoples) around 1225. Of Gujarat he wrote that its products 'comprise great quantities of indigo, red kino, myrobolans and foreign cotton stuffs of every colour', and that these goods were shipped every year to the Arab lands (Ta shï) for sale.
events.significance: Independent Chinese evidence that Gujarat was a major exporter of indigo to the Islamic world before European involvement.

sources.quote: The native products comprise great quantities of indigo, red kino, myrobolans and foreign cotton stuffs of every colour. Every year these goods are transported to the Ta shï countries for sale.

events.title: Marco Polo describes indigo-making at Quilon
events.place: Coilum (Kollam/Quilon), Kerala, India
events.summary: Marco Polo reported that Coilum had 'abundance of very fine indigo', made by steeping a herb in great vessels of water until it decomposed, then letting the liquid set in the hot sun. The indigo was cut into pieces of four ounces each for export to Europe. He also noted indigo in Gujarat and 'in great abundance' at Cambay. His editor Henry Yule judged that the account 'does describe the chief features of the manufacture of Indigo by fermentation'.
events.significance: The first detailed European eyewitness description of indigo production in India.

events.title: Thuringia's woad towns and Erfurt's university
events.place: Erfurt, Thuringia, Germany
events.summary: Between the 13th and 16th centuries woad shaped Thuringia's economy more than any other crop. A contiguous growing zone formed between Erfurt, Langensalza, Gotha, Arnstadt and Weimar. Erfurt, with Gotha, Arnstadt, Langensalza and Tennstedt, formed the five Thuringian 'woad towns' that processed and traded the crop. A local history source says woad wealth is 'presumably' what let Erfurt's citizens pay for founding their university, which opened in 1392.
events.significance: The clearest German example of woad money building urban institutions.

events.title: Toulouse's 'land of cocagne' woad boom begins
events.place: Toulouse and the Lauragais, Languedoc, France
events.summary: Toulouse's exports of pastel (woad) grew from the mid-14th century on English demand. The trade's golden age ran from 1463 to 1562. The Lauragais became Europe's leading woad district, nicknamed the 'pays de cocagne' after the cocagnes (balls of crushed woad leaves), and Toulouse became the hub of the trade. Most of the boom falls after 1497.
events.significance: Europe's largest woad economy on the eve of the sea route to India, which would eventually undercut it with imported indigo.

events.title: Kano's Kofar Mata dye pits (traditional date)
events.place: Kofar Mata, old city of Kano, Nigeria
events.summary: A Google Arts & Culture story by the Centenary Project says the Kofar Mata indigo dye pits in Kano were established in 1498, near the city's central mosque and the historic Kofar Mata gate, and that there are over 100 pits. The date comes from tradition rather than excavation; Wikipedia says only that the pits' origins are commonly traced back more than 500 years. It falls one year after this slice's 1497 cut-off.
events.significance: Africa's best-known surviving indigo dye pits tie Hausa textile production of the late 15th century to the present.

notes:
CONVENTIONS: 'year' is a representative integer (negative = BCE). era is 'origins' for before 500 CE and 'medieval' for 500-1497. verificationStatus is CONFIRMED when the fetched page states the claim; PENDING when the source is right but was not read in full (paywall, HTTP 403/429, or seen only as a search snippet) or when the only source is Wikipedia; DERIVED when the researcher computed, counted or translated the value. All pages were accessed 2026-09-23. Wikipedia 'date' fields give the access year.

LOCATION PRECISION. Actual site (verified coordinates): huaca-prieta, beycesultan, tutankhamun (KV62), hallstatt (salt mine), oseberg (mound), shosoin, calakmul, chichen-itza (Sacred Cenote), marco-polo (Kollam), tellem (Bandiagara Escarpment centroid). Approximate city or site coordinates from general knowledge: york-coppergate, amiens, erfurt, toulouse, jerusalem, qayrawan, fustat, kano (Kofar Mata placed at old-city Kano, about 12.00N 8.51E; not verified). Representative only, because the source gives no findspot or the event is a text: egypt-fifth-dynasty (Saqqara), babylonian tablet (Babylon), xunzi (Lanling, approximate), caesar (Canterbury for Cantium), periplus (Banbhore, one proposed site of Barbarikon), pliny (Rome), diocletian edict (Nicomedia), qimin-yaoshu (Shouguang), capitulare (Aachen), zhao-rugua (Khambhat/Cambay).

KEY CAVEATS AND DISPUTES.
(1) Huaca Prieta: Splitstoser et al. put the oldest indigo cloth at about 6,200-6,000 years old, inferred from strata bracketed at 6882-6657 and 5848-5585 cal BP. The year -4200 is representative.
(2) Egypt, Fifth Dynasty (c. 2400 BCE): cited only as 'earliest reported' in the Science Advances and National Geographic pieces. No findspot or primary report was located, and whether the blue is woad or Indigofera is unknown; PROTA says both were known in Egypt.
(3) Tutankhamun: spectroscopy (and HPLC generally) identifies indigotin, not the plant source.
(4) Babylonian dye tablet (BM 62788+82978, 1882,0918.2757): the British Museum page returned 403, so its wording is from a search snippet (PENDING). Koren (2022) calls the tablet 'Late Babylonian' and dates it to the seventh century BCE. The blue dyestuff is not named in the tablet; 'probably woad' is Koren's editorial insertion. The published edition of one fragment is Leichty 1979 (AOAT 203), not read.
(5) Caesar, Gallic War 5.14, 'vitro inficiunt': vitrum usually means glass. Pyatt et al. (1991, 'Non isatis sed vitrum') argued for copper or iron pigments from Lindow Man analyses; Carr (2005) argued for woad tattooing. Dantas (2023) and Hoecherl consider it unresolved.
(6) Pliny: the Bostock/Perseus chapter is 35.27, which is 35.46 in Loeb section numbering (the brief's 'NH 35.46'). The 20 denarii/lb (77 CE) and Diocletian's 750 denarii/lb (301 CE) cannot be compared directly because of 3rd-century inflation and debasement. The edict's indigo entry is marked '(?)' by the translator.
(7) Maya Blue dates conflict. The Wheaton/Field Museum release says it was used c. 300-1500 CE, but Calakmul analyses place the earliest use in the Late Preclassic. The Calakmul paper (J. Cultural Heritage 2011, doi 10.1016/j.culher.2009.12.002) was not read; the 'c. 300 BC-300 AD' gloss is from a search snippet. The Sacred Cenote blue layer is 14 ft in the release but about 5 m (16 ft) in Wikipedia. Bonampak murals were not researched.
(8) Hallstatt: the 33% and 58% indigotin shares come from a paywalled abstract (PENDING); the NHM Vienna pages confirm woad in general. Hochdorf and Hohmichele 'woad-dyed textiles' appear in Wikipedia with [citation needed] and could not be verified, so they are dropped. Heuneburg woad-seed impressions (Wikipedia ref) are also unverified.
(9) Neolithic woad seeds, Adaouste/l'Audoste cave (Bouches-du-Rhône): only a general statement from Cambridge University Botanic Garden ('Seeds have been found in caves in France dating back to the Neolithic period') and an uncited Wikipedia line. No date was found, so there is no event. The relevant paper, Zech-Matterne & Leconte 2010 (Veget. Hist. Archaeobot. 19:137-142, doi 10.1007/s00334-009-0229-3), could not be read.
(10) Dropped for lack of evidence: Çatalhöyük indigo (nothing found); Indus Valley / Mohenjo-daro indigo or dye vats (no verified evidence of indigo; PROTA's 'oldest Sanskrit records' line is too vague to date).
(11) Oseberg: the woad seed box is attested by Store norske leksikon. The primary report, Holmboe 1927 in Osebergfundet vol. 5, was not read. Britannica dates the ship itself to about 820; tree rings date the burial to 834.
(12) York: Tomlinson 1985 (J. Arch. Sci. 12:269-283) identified dyeplants at Coppergate but is paywalled and was not read. The EAU report quoted refers to mid-to-late 11th-century deposits. The Wikipedia claim of a 10th-century 'dye shop with woad and madder' was not verified.
(13) Geniza: the 978 record (T-S 12.468) describes the goods in Hebrew as 'isatis called Syrian nil' (researcher's reading), so this 'indigo' may be a woad-type product. PGP descriptions rely on Moshe Gil's editions. Goitein's broader discussions of the indigo trade were not consulted.
(14) Benjamin of Tudela names Jewish dyers but never the dyestuffs; linking them to indigo is contextual.
(15) Frederick II and Sicily: Yule's note (Gutenberg) says 'Indigo had been introduced into Sicily by the Jews during the time of Frederick II'. The specific claim that Jews from Garbum/Jerba were invited to Palermo in 1239-40 to grow indigo and henna appeared only in search snippets (source unidentified), so no event was created.
(16) Other medieval trade leads, in Yule's notes but not independently verified: Pegolotti's merchant handbook names the finest indigo 'Indaco Baccadeo' (from Baghdad), and Barcelona tariffs list 'Indigo de Bagadel'. 13th-century London Painters' Guild bylaws (Liber Horn) forbade painting on gold or silver with 'inde de Baldas'.
(17) Erfurt: the University of Erfurt received its papal charter in 1379 and opened in 1392. The idea that woad paid for it is hedged ('Vermutlich', presumably) by the local-history source. The '3 tons of gold a year' and '300 woad villages' figures seen in search results are unsourced and omitted. The 49 villages (1579) figure is post-period context.
(18) Toulouse: the golden age (1463-1562) falls mostly after 1497. The 40,000 tonnes/year figure is a tourism-board claim with no scholarly citation; Brumont 1994 (Annales du Midi) would hold the real export series but its full text could not be retrieved. The Hôtel d'Assézat (1555) is post-period and not verified here.
(19) Kano Kofar Mata 1498 is a traditional date; the founder name 'Muhammad Dabosa' in some web sources is unverified. It is one year outside the slice and included only because the brief asked for it.
(20) Woad vs Indigofera yield: the only peer-reviewed ratio found is Dupré et al. 2025, about 0.2% vs 1% extraction yield (five times). The widely repeated 'woad yields one-thirtieth' claim was found only on blogs and is not verified. Modern yields vary widely with method (Hartl et al. 2024).
(21) China: the Xia xiaozheng line '五月啟灌藍蓼' (quoted in Qimin yaoshu ch. 53) may be earlier than Xunzi, but its date is uncertain, so no event was made. The claim of Chinese indigo 'c. 3000 BCE' (JSTOR Daily) is unsourced and omitted, and no early Chinese textile dye analysis (e.g. Mawangdui) was verified. ctext.org states that it does not authorise automated access, so Chinese texts were read on Wikisource instead.
(22) Japan: only the Nara-period Shōsōin evidence is included; Heian sources such as the Engishiki dye recipes were not researched.
(23) Access failures: the British Museum, ScienceDirect, Academia.edu, MDPI (403), the Met (429), Kew POWO and UNESCO could not be fetched. The MDPI article by Dupré et al. was read in full through the Europe PMC REST API (PMC12348740).
